summary: This memo presents a security labeling framework for the Internet, intended to help protocol designers decide what, if any, labeling their protocols should support. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Secret documents get labels like confidential. This paper helps designers decide whether and how network messages should have such labels.

questions: how do security labels work in networks
subtitle: A framework for attaching security labels to network data

tldr.problem: Network protocols need a way to mark data with its security requirements—like confidentiality level or integrity needs—so that systems en route know how to handle it safely.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a framework where data can carry explicit labels (bits in the packet header) or implicit labels (inferred from context), at any of the seven OSI network layers, with rules for how each layer handles them.
tldr.outcome: Protocol designers can use this framework to decide whether and where their protocols should support labeling. The framework supports both integrity models (like Biba) and confidentiality models (like Bell and LaPadula).

facts.label: Label encoding modes
facts.value: Explicit or Implicit, Connectionless or Connection-oriented

today: RFC 1457 is informational and has not been updated or obsoleted. Security labeling in Internet protocols remains an area of protocol design choice; the framework provides guidance but does not mandate any standard syntax.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1457 presents a framework for security labeling in network protocols. The framework is not a standard itself, but guidance for protocol designers and network architects. It answers the question: should my protocol support security labels, and if so, where should they go and what should they say?

The memo uses the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Reference Model to organize the discussion, so OSI protocol designers and Internet architects can both apply it. Security labels are one mechanism for protecting data; they work best combined with encryption, authentication, and access control.
sections.eli5: When you send secret data over the network, computers need to know it's secret so they don't send it somewhere unsafe. This explains how to mark data with a security label.

sections.title: Security Label Types and Models
sections.content:
The RFC identifies two kinds of security labels, each addressing a different protection goal. Integrity labels tell how much confidence to place in data. They are based on the Biba model: data can only be written by trusted entities with equal or higher integrity. When low-integrity data is processed, everything it touches is downgraded. Sensitivity labels tell how much damage would result from disclosure. They are based on the Bell and LaPadula model: high-sensitivity data can only be read by authorized processes, and can only be copied to containers where secrecy is guaranteed. Anything processed alongside high-sensitivity data must be treated as high-sensitivity.

Both models rely on attaching the label as an attribute of the data itself. The label must travel with the data through the network, bound to it by cryptographic integrity protection. Without binding, someone could strip or modify labels in transit.
sections.eli5: Some labels say "this data came from a trusted source, trust it." Others say "this data is secret, protect it." Both kinds travel with the data so every computer knows what to do.

sections.title: Where to Place Labels in the OSI Stack
sections.content:
The RFC examines each of the seven OSI layers to determine where labels can and should be placed. Physical and session layers offer limited options. Data Link and Network layers are best for labels that drive routing decisions (bridges and routers). Transport layer labels are best for end-to-end handling requirements but require connection-oriented protocols. Application layer labels let protocols define labels specific to their use case without burdening others.

End systems (hosts) and intermediate systems (routers, bridges) have different requirements. Intermediate systems can work with small fixed-format labels in the header to make routing decisions quickly. End systems often need larger variable-length labels to express complete handling requirements. When security labels appear in high protocol layers (transport, application, or above), intermediate systems cannot use them for routing decisions, which limits their utility for network-wide protection.
sections.eli5: You can put a label in different places in a network message. Some places are good for quick decisions (like routing), others are good for telling the destination computer how to protect the data.

sections.title: Explicit and Implicit Labels
sections.content:
Labels can be explicit (actual bits in the protocol header) or implicit (inferred from some other attribute like the physical port or the encryption key used). The IP Security Option (IPSO) is an example of explicit network-layer labeling. Explicit labels are predictable and parseable but consume header space. Implicit labels save space but require complex logic to determine them from context.

Labels can also be connectionless (appearing in every packet) or connection-oriented (set once at connection establishment, inherited by all data). Connectionless labeling works with any transport, but can consume significant header space. Connection-oriented labeling is more efficient when a connection carries data of uniform sensitivity, but only works with connection-based protocols like TCP.
sections.eli5: You can write the label in the message (explicit) or let the computer figure it out from the message type (implicit). You can write it on every message (connectionless) or just once at the start (connection-oriented).

sections.title: Design Guidelines
sections.content:
The RFC offers four guidelines for protocol designers. First, use explicit labels in Data Link or Network layers for label-based routing decisions. Second, put application-specific labels in the application protocol itself, so other applications are not burdened. Third, use Network or Transport layer labels for trusted demultiplexing (handing data to the right process based on its label). Fourth, to avoid needing translation between different label formats, design a common explicit label syntax where many security policies can be registered, so all systems understand the same format.

The framework emphasizes that security labels are not a complete solution. They must work alongside other mechanisms: encryption to bind the label to the data, digital signatures to verify the source, and robust access control logic on end systems. The RFC acknowledges that very few hard rules exist; protocol designers face many tradeoffs in choosing where and how to implement labeling.
sections.eli5: If you're designing a protocol, here are four tips: use routing labels at the network level, keep special labels in the right protocol layer, use labels to deliver data to the right process, and try to use the same label format everywhere.
